title: East Fire Island: Native Coastal Homeland and Changing Land Control
summary: East Fire Island sits within a living Native coastal homeland. English colonial claims and later federal ownership show changing forms of control over the bay; public conservation did not itself return land or jurisdiction to Native people.
address_label: East Fire Island, Great South Bay — modern island context
map_geometry_source: Modern project coastline; NPS 2015 Map 3-C, published GNIS point and visual basemap cross-check. Not a historical deed survey.
why_this_matters: A colonial patent and a public park inventory record different claims to land. Reading them alongside Native continuance prevents government conservation from being mistaken for Indigenous land return.
introduction_title: A coastal homeland under changing control
introduction_content: East Fire Island sits within a living Native coastal homeland. English colonial claims and later federal ownership show changing forms of control over the bay; public conservation did not itself return land or jurisdiction to Native people.
history_title: Colonial claims, public conservation and continuing Native relationships
history_content:
A bay island, not the ocean beach

East Fire Island lies in Great South Bay, east of West Fire Island and north of the outer barrier near Ocean Beach. It is a separate island, not the eastern end of the long Fire Island barrier. Its marshes belong to the connected coastal landscape through which people traveled, gathered food and sustained relationships. Fire Island Draft General Management Plan / Environmental Impact Statement: Map 3-C, Transportation

Native relationships came before property boundaries

The National Park Service describes Fire Island and surrounding waters through the long histories of Unkechaug, Secatogue and Shinnecock people. Seasonal settlement and coastal harvesting preceded colonial settlement. Native people continue to care for this coast, including through the Unkechaug community at Poospatuck. That wider history gives this island its setting; it does not establish the location of a particular settlement on it. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore

An English governor claimed power to grant the bay islands

On June 4, 1688, Thomas Dongan, the English royal governor of New York, issued William Nicoll a patent for bay islands between an inlet and Nicoll’s lands at the Connetquot River. The later Nicoll v. Trustees opinion examined those words and the problem of shifting inlets. A Crown patent was an assertion of colonial authority over land. It must not be confused with proof that every Native right was surrendered, or with a Native deed naming each island on today’s map. Nicoll v. Trustees, 1 Johns. Ch. 166

What remains unresolved about this island’s early transfer

The cited patent record provides regional context, not a complete chain of ownership for East Fire Island. The sources checked here do not establish the terms of an island-specific Native agreement or trace every later private transfer. Nor does the 1814 decision about the disputed western islands settle East Fire Island’s title. The separate Captree chapter explains that litigation and the named Native parties in a different beach agreement. Nicoll v. Trustees, 1 Johns. Ch. 166

Congress brought bay islands into a national seashore boundary

The September 11, 1964 law authorized the Secretary of the Interior to establish Fire Island National Seashore to conserve beaches, dunes and other natural features. Its boundary language already named bay islands, including Sexton, West and Hollins, as well as surrounding waters. Inclusion in a park boundary and government ownership are different: this law alone does not tell us when a particular parcel changed hands. Public Law 88-587: Fire Island National Seashore

By 1977, a federal inventory recorded ownership

The National Park Service’s administrative history reports that its 1977 inventory counted East Fire Island and its satellite islands as federally owned in fee. The inventory grouped them together at 156 acres; that figure is not the area of this modern outline. This documents federal control by 1977, without claiming that acquisition occurred in that year or that the islands had one uninterrupted private title. Land Regulation at Fire Island National Seashore: A History and Analysis, 1964–2004

Conservation is not the end of the Native story

Public conservation can limit development, but a change to federal ownership is not, by itself, LandBack. Returning Indigenous authority, access and relationships with land and water requires a different set of commitments. The continuing Native stewardship described by the National Park Service matters here: this is a living coastal homeland, not an empty landscape whose human history began with a park boundary. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore

Read next: Captree’s Native agreements and competing claims, West Fire Island’s private parcels and federal acquisition, and the continuing Unkechaug homeland at Poospatuck.
whereintheworld_content: This approximate outline follows the project’s modern East Fire Island coastline, checked against National Park Service Map 3-C, its published GNIS location and the visible basemap. It is a reading area for the island’s history, not a surveyed Native conveyance, the full 1688 patent, or a federal acquisition parcel. The 1977 inventory includes satellite islands that are not all inside this outline. Marsh edges change. The outline does not identify a landing place or grant access.
